surfaces.part: cornice strip with brown cap at the top
door or lower panel with blue glass

answer.evidence: All 16 rows are full width, so there is no ellipse and no widening or narrowing in the silhouette. Rows 0-4 are a flat horizontal cornice band (brown row 0, dark row 1, tan row 2, cream rows 3-4) drawn as a front-facing strip. There is no lighter or darker front-edge line followed by eave shadow, and no sloped roof plane. Row 5 is a dark outline separating it from the wall. Rows 6-10 are vertical window faces (teal and white), rows 11-12 are a dark band, and rows 13-15 are a blue panel or door. Everything is a vertical face, so the piece reads as a flat front elevation with no visible top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny striped-awning or stall icon, about 16x12 source pixels. It has no tile roof, no walls and no door or windows, so it is not a whole building like the two references, which are full houses with scalloped tile roofs, timber or stone walls and doors. It shows only about 3 lightness steps (teal, white, a dark base) against roughly 5-6 per material in the references. The awning stripes and small body are simple blocks with no tile scallops, plaster speckle or stone shading. The measured 0% neutral edge pixels shows the outline is tinted rather than black, and the 0% near-flat coverage and 15 visible tones come from a very small, high-contrast piece. These do not make up for the lack of structure. Next to the references it looks much thinner and more sticker-like, and it is the wrong kind of object for this comparison.
